subject: Career
title: Slack Etiquette and Async Communication
description: A fast breakdown of Slack Etiquette and Async Communication for builders.

hook.text: 'Hey.' That's it. The message. Now you're waiting, anxious, for whatever comes next. Don't be that person.

buildup.text: Async communication means people respond on their schedule. Your message must be self-contained.

discovery.text: The best Slack messages include: context, question, and what you've already tried — all in one message.

twist.text: 'No hello' is a movement. Leading with the full question respects everyone's time.

climax.text: Use threads, not channels, for discussions. Tag only who needs to act. Use reactions to acknowledge.

punchline.text: Good async messages don't need follow-ups. They're complete on arrival.

quiz.question: What makes a good async Slack message?
options: Context, question, and what you've tried — all in one message

details.summary: Asynchronous communication tools like Slack require deliberate etiquette to prevent notification overload, context fragmentation, and the expectation of instant replies. Establishing team norms around channel usage, threading, and response windows preserves deep work time.
details.whyItMatters: Workers check messaging tools an average of every six minutes, destroying focus. Clear async norms protect productivity while maintaining team connectivity.
takeaways: Use threads consistently to keep channels scannable for everyone
Set explicit response-time expectations per channel urgency level
Batch non-urgent messages to reduce interrupt-driven workflows

faq.question: What are reasonable response time expectations for Slack messages?
faq.answer: Urgent channels can expect responses within thirty minutes during work hours. General channels should allow two to four hours. Informational channels require no immediate response. Publishing these norms explicitly in channel descriptions reduces anxiety.

faq.question: How do I reduce Slack distractions without missing important messages?
faq.answer: Mute low-priority channels and check them in batches. Configure keyword notifications for truly urgent terms. Use scheduled Do Not Disturb windows during deep work blocks. Most messages genuinely do not require immediate attention.
